modals.text:
Business & Economy in the Age of AI
Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.
Close

Writing Art's Histories
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
Close

Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
Close

AI Ethics
AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.
Close

Introduction to Biodiversity
Introduces the diversity of living organisms, from bacteria and archaea to protists, plants, fungi and animals. Students examine evolutionary relationships, distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement, supported by a small project on a selected branch of the tree of life.
Close

Conservation Biology
Examines human-driven biodiversity loss and approaches to conservation. Students study habitat destruction, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change and extinction, followed by conservation planning and species management. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
Close

The Science of Evolution
Examines evolution from genes to populations, including its history, mechanisms and theoretical and practical study. It develops evolutionary explanations of biological diversity and change.
Close

Functional Anatomy
Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Medical images, anatomical drawing, human-specimen material and guided practicals develop spatial reasoning, including observation in a dissection room. Historical, ethical and societal questions accompany these academic learning activities, which do not provide clinical qualification.
Close

Psycholinguistics
Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
Close

Accounting & Corporate Finance
Accounting & Corporate Finance introduces financial and management accounting, financial-statement preparation and analysis, costing, pricing, budgeting and organisational control. Students assess investment decisions using accounting measures, discounted cash flow, net present value, internal rate of return and cost of capital. A case study examines the misuse of an accounting principle and its effects on financial statements.
Close

Consumer Product Design
You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
Close

Principles of Private Law
Examines principles of property, tort and contract law and other selected areas of private law. It compares legal systems including Germany, France, England, China and the United States, and considers the social, economic and political pressures underlying legal principles.
Close

R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
Close

Money, Banking & Finance
Examines financial markets, commercial banks and central banks, including interest rates, financial regulation, financial crises and monetary policy. Students analyse financial problems and manage a simulated bank in the Stanford Banking Game, using Excel dashboards and financial forecasts to inform decisions about loans, deposits, capital, liquidity and risk.
Close

Creative Communication Laboratory
Creative Communication Laboratory combines close reading and creative workshops with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop traditional or hybrid creative projects grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require them to explain their formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
Close

Persuasive Communication
Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.
Close

Public Economics
Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
Close
